title: Needlestick injury from an HIV-positive patient: first aid and PEP

header.contentArea: Professionalism and patient safety: occupational exposure to blood-borne viruses
guidelineVersions: BHIVA/BASHH UK guideline for the use of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis 2021 (current Sep 2026)
UKHSA Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (issued November 2023; updated Jul 2026)
UKHSA Green Book chapter 18: Hepatitis B (5 February 2026)

related.why: Another theatre safety station: digital block and local anaesthetic doses

brief.scenario: You are assisting at an open small bowel resection. While closing, a curved suture needle passes through both your gloves into your left index finger, and it bleeds. The patient is known to be HIV-positive.
brief.task: Tell the examiner what you would do immediately, and answer questions on risk assessment, post-exposure prophylaxis and follow-up.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: First aid, report now, risk assess, PEP within hours if indicated, then hepatitis B and C and follow-up.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Finishing the list first. Delay costs PEP efficacy.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd tell the surgeon, step away safely once someone takes over, and wash the wound under running water with soap."

grid.label: First aid
grid.fail: Squeezes or sucks the wound, scrubs it with caustic agents, or keeps operating.
grid.pass: Tells the surgeon, hands over safely, removes gloves, washes under running water with soap, covers with a waterproof dressing.
grid.high: Knows squeezing is not recommended; irrigates eyes or mouth with water or saline for a splash; patient safety maintained while someone rescrubs.

grid.label: Report urgently
grid.fail: Waits until the end of the list or next day for occupational health.
grid.pass: Reports at once to occupational health, or the emergency department out of hours; completes an incident report.
grid.high: Occupational health follow-up within 72 hours; exposure to a BBV-positive source is reported to HSE (RIDDOR) and UKHSA surveillance.

grid.label: Risk assessment
grid.fail: Quotes a percentage and stops, or never asks about the source's treatment.
grid.pass: Asks depth, visible blood, needle type, and the source's ART, adherence and latest viral load.
grid.high: Risk about 0.3% from an untreated source; deep injury raises it. On ART for 6 months, undetectable: PEP generally not indicated.

grid.label: PEP: when and what (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Says PEP only works within 1 hour, or can start after a week; waits for results.
grid.pass: Starts as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours, not beyond 72 hours; does not wait for source or baseline results.
grid.high: First line: tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine plus raltegravir 1200 mg once daily for 28 days; checks interactions and pregnancy.

grid.label: Hepatitis B and C
grid.pass: Checks own hepatitis B immunity; source tested for hepatitis B and C; baseline hepatitis C testing for the recipient.
grid.high: Source status unknown: responder, consider booster. If source HBsAg-positive and non-immune: vaccine plus HBIG, ideally within 48 h, no later than 1 week.

grid.label: Testing the source patient
grid.fail: Asks the patient for consent himself, or tests without consent.
grid.pass: Another staff member seeks consent for HIV, hepatitis B and C testing; source testing must not delay PEP.
grid.high: If the patient lacks capacity, tests only if in the patient's best interests; keeps the exposure confidential and documented.

grid.label: Follow-up and advice
grid.fail: Gives no follow-up plan or advice.
grid.pass: Baseline HIV, renal and liver tests; occupational health follow-up; HIV test at least 45 days after finishing PEP.
grid.high: Advises condoms until follow-up testing is negative, adherence, side effects, and to report symptoms of seroconversion.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The needle has gone through your gloves. What do you do?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd squeeze it to make it bleed, change gloves and finish closing. I'd go to occupational health tomorrow.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It has to be within an hour or it doesn't work, so it's probably too late by tomorrow.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, it's HIV that matters here.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How would you find out more about the patient?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd ask him myself after surgery if I can test his blood.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: If I feel fine, nothing more.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The needle has gone through your gloves. What do you do?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd tell the surgeon, step away once someone takes over, take my gloves off and wash the finger under running water with soap. No squeezing. Then a waterproof dressing.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd report it straight away to occupational health, or the emergency department out of hours, and fill in an incident report.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How do you assess the risk?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: How deep, whether there was visible blood, the type of needle, and the patient's treatment, adherence and latest viral load.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: He was diagnosed three weeks ago and has not started treatment. Viral load 45,000.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Then I need PEP, as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours and not beyond 72. I wouldn't wait for his tests or my baseline bloods.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hepatitis B and C. I'd check my hepatitis B immunity and have baseline hepatitis C testing.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Someone else from the team should ask him for consent to test for HIV, hepatitis B and C.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Baseline HIV, kidney and liver tests, occupational health follow-up, and an HIV test at least 45 days after finishing PEP.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Wash under running water with soap; squeezing isn't recommended. If blood had splashed my eye I'd irrigate with water or saline. The patient stays safe: someone rescrubs before I leave.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How quickly will you be seen?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Today, for PEP. Occupational health should follow me up within 72 hours. Because he has a blood-borne virus, the exposure is reportable to HSE and to UKHSA surveillance.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: About 0.3% from an untreated source; a deep injury with visible blood raises it. If he'd been on treatment for six months with an undetectable load, PEP generally wouldn't be indicated, though a deep injury could still be discussed case by case.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Tenofovir disoproxil with emtricitabine, plus raltegravir 1200 mg once daily, for 28 days. I'd check interactions such as antacids and iron, and pregnancy status where relevant.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Your last hepatitis B antibody level was protective.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Then I'm a known responder. His hepatitis B status is unknown, so I'd consider a booster, as my last dose was over a year ago; no immunoglobulin. If he turned out to be HBsAg-positive and I weren't immune, I'd need vaccine plus HBIG, ideally within 48 hours and no later than a week.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Then consent waits until he can decide, unless testing is in his best interests. It mustn't delay my PEP. I'd keep it confidential and document it.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Until my follow-up test is negative I'd use condoms, take every dose, and report any flu-like illness or rash.

failures.move: Believing PEP is futile after 1 hour, or waiting for source results.
failures.consequence: PEP is started late or not at all when it could still work.

failures.move: Finishing the list and reporting the next day.
failures.consequence: Hours lost in the window when PEP is most effective.

failures.move: Squeezing the wound or scrubbing it with bleach.
failures.consequence: Tissue damage with no proven benefit.
Misses hepatitis B prophylaxis and hepatitis C follow-up.

recovery.when: Asked 'Is it too late for PEP?'
recovery.line: Not within 72 hours. Sooner is better, so I'd start it today.

recovery.when: Asked about a patient on suppressed treatment
recovery.line: PEP is generally not indicated, but I'd still get urgent expert advice for a deep injury.

knowledge.fact: Wash with soap and running water; do not squeeze. Irrigate mucosa with water.
HIV risk from a sharps injury, untreated source: about 0.3%. Deep injury and visible blood raise it.
Source on ART at least 6 months, undetectable: PEP generally not indicated after sharps; case by case.
Start PEP preferably within 24 hours, not beyond 72. Tenofovir disoproxil/emtricitabine plus raltegravir 1200 mg once daily, 28 days.
Final HIV test at least 45 days after completing PEP.
Hepatitis B, HBsAg-positive source: non-immune gets vaccine plus HBIG, ideally within 48 h, no later than 1 week.
Unknown source: responder, consider booster; HBIG only for known non-responders.

sources.version: 2021 guideline, published 2022; current version on BHIVA site September 2026
sources.supports: First aid; occupational health within 72 hours and reporting; 0.3% sharps risk and risk factors; PEP indications by source viral load; timing (preferably 24 h, not beyond 72 h); first-line regimen and 28-day course; source consent by another staff member and best-interests testing; baseline tests; HIV test at least 45 days after PEP; condom advice

sources.name: UK Health Security Agency. Immunoglobulin: when to use. Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (issued November 2023)
sources.supports: Exposure to a known HBsAg-positive source: fully vaccinated, booster (no HBIG) unless boosted within the past year; non-responders HBIG plus vaccine; HBIG with vaccine as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours, ideally within 48 hours, no later than a week

sources.name: UK Health Security Agency. Immunisation against infectious disease (the Green Book), chapter 18: Hepatitis B
sources.supports: Table 18.8: unknown source, fully vaccinated: consider booster if last dose 1 year or more ago; unvaccinated: accelerated vaccine course; known non-responder: HBIG plus booster

sources.name: Health and Safety Executive. Sharps injuries: actions to take (RIDDOR)
sources.supports: Injury from a sharp known to be contaminated with a blood-borne virus is reportable to HSE as a dangerous occurrence

partner.opening: A suture needle has gone through both your gloves into your finger, and it is bleeding. The patient is HIV-positive. What do you do?

reveals.finding: Solid curved needle, through double gloves, moderately deep, visible blood on the needle.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about the source's treatment
reveals.finding: Diagnosed three weeks ago, not yet on ART. Viral load 45,000 copies/ml. Hepatitis B and C status unknown.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about own hepatitis B status
reveals.finding: Completed vaccination; documented protective antibody level two years ago; no booster since.

push.question: What do you do first?
push.expect: Hand over safely, wash with soap and running water, no squeezing.

push.question: Who do you tell and when?
push.expect: Occupational health or ED now; incident report.

push.question: What determines the risk?
push.expect: Depth, blood, needle type; source ART, adherence, viral load.

push.question: When must PEP start, and what is it?
push.expect: Preferably within 24 h, not beyond 72 h; TDF/FTC plus raltegravir 1200 mg once daily, 28 days.

push.question: What about hepatitis?
push.expect: Own HBV immunity, source HBV/HCV testing, HBV booster or HBIG as indicated.

push.question: How is the source tested?
push.expect: Consent sought by another staff member; best interests if no capacity.

push.question: What follow-up do you need?
push.expect: Baseline tests; HIV test at least 45 days after PEP; condoms until negative.

curveballs.prompt: He has been on ART for 3 years with an undetectable viral load last month.
curveballs.safeAnswer: PEP generally not indicated after a sharps injury; discuss case by case with an HIV clinician given the depth.

curveballs.prompt: It is now 80 hours since the injury.
curveballs.safeAnswer: PEP is not started beyond 72 hours; arrange baseline and follow-up testing and support.

curveballs.prompt: Your consultant says to finish closing first.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explain PEP is time-critical; someone else closes; report now.
Pregnancy does not change the decision to start PEP; the raltegravir dose changes to 400 mg twice daily; seek HIV specialist advice.
